The driver's claimed justification (chat #3) is not supported by the traffic record: there is no traffic incident anywhere near the route in the trip window, and Ayer Rajah Expressway was only band 4 (30–39 km/h), not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires.

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $7.26 (model confidence 0.86)
events.body:
This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (F6: base $3.90, distance $20.43 for 14.5 km, time $5.76, platform $1.47, total $31.56), so unlike a fixed-quote service, extra distance driven flows into the fare and the RD-2 metered branch applies [F6][RD-2]. The GPS record shows a single off-route segment, 14:27-14:37, covering 6.47 km where the optimal route covers 1.32 km, adding 5.15 km and straying up to 1194 m from the optimal route [F3][RD-1]. RD-1 sets no threshold, so this unexplained deviation breaches the driver's duty to take the shortest and most direct route [F3][RD-1].

RD-5 cannot exempt the segment. The driver's request (go round via West Coast Highway, 14:29) and the rider's reply (Sure, go ahead, 14:30) both post-date the segment start at 14:27, so the agreement did not precede leaving the optimal route [F7][F8][F3][RD-5]; the driver's statement to the same effect is consistent but does not cure the ordering [F9][RD-5].

RD-4 does not exempt the segment either. No traffic incident was recorded near the route in the trip window [F12], so RD-4(a) is not met; the only congestion evidence is AYE band 4 (30-39 km/h), which is not band 1-2 severe congestion and in any case is corroborative only and cannot exempt a segment alone [F10][RD-4]. RD-3 does not apply: the rider never named a stop, so this is a driver-proposed reroute assessed under RD-5, not a rider-requested stop [F7][F3][RD-3].

claims.assertion: The trip was a RydeTAXI metered ride, so extra distance on an unexcused detour flows straight into the fare; the meter billed 14.5 km against an optimal 8.6 km, i.e. +5.9 km (+69%), and the fare shows distance $20.43 for 14.5 km.

GPS records one off-route segment 14:27–14:37 covering 6.47 km where the optimal route covers 1.32 km, adding 5.15 km and straying up to 1194 m from the optimal route — an unexcused deviation absent any exemption.

The rider's consent (chat #2 at 14:30) came after the deviation had already started at 14:27, so under the 'before you go' rule it cannot excuse the segment; the driver's own message (chat #1 at 14:29) was also only sent after he had turned off.

The driver's claimed justification (chat #3) is not supported by the traffic record: there is no traffic incident anywhere near the route in the trip window, and Ayer Rajah Expressway was only band 4 (30–39 km/h), not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires.
RydeTAXI refund on the unexcused segment = 5.15 extra_km × the trip's per-km rate (distance fare $20.43 ÷ 14.5 km = $1.4090/km, consistent with the $1.41/km billed rate) = $7.256 ≈ $7.26.
The driver already has one upheld dispute in the last 90 days, so this further upheld route deviation makes his conduct repeated and warrants a separate account review alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The rider did reply 'Sure, go ahead' (F8), and the driver will argue this was a mutual agreement to the West Coast Highway routing; our answer rests only on the timestamp ordering (F8 14:30 vs segment start 14:27 in F3), which the driver may contest.

The traffic record does show congestion building on Ayer Rajah Expressway, band 4 (F10), which the driver will use as a 'reasonable cause' argument even though it falls short of the band 1–2 threshold in RD-4(b).
The rider's own profile shows 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld (F14), which the other side may use to suggest a pattern of unfounded complaints.
The refund is limited to the 5.15 km segment excess; the remaining 0.75 km gap between that figure and the 5.9 km total (F1) is treated as matching residue and is not recoverable under RD-2.

claims.assertion: The only off-route segment in the GPS record is the single deviation from 14:27 to 14:37 (6.47 km driven vs 1.32 km on the optimal route, +5.15 km), and it is the sole source of the +5.9 km / +69% total excess over the 8.6 km optimal route.

The rider expressly agreed to the alternative route: the driver asked at 14:29 whether he could go round via West Coast Highway and the rider replied 'Sure, go ahead' at 14:30; the driver's own statement is consistent with that exchange.

The rider's agreement message (14:30) is not timestamped after the start of the off-route segment (14:27), so the consent does not qualify under the strict 'before you go' test in RD-5 and the segment cannot be fully exempted on consent alone.

No traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (14:11–14:48), so the congestion described by the driver does not meet the incident-based exemption of RD-4(a); the AYE speed band 4 record showing only moderate 30–39 km/h flow cannot stand alone as a justified-reroute exemption, and RD-4(b) itself does not permit standalone exemption.

The trip is a RydeTAXI metered fare billed on actual distance, so the refund under RD-2 is confined to the meter units of the unexempted deviation: 5.15 km of extra mileage at the trip's per-km rate of $1.41/km (= distance fare $20.43 ÷ 14.5 km) gives $7.26, not the $8.35 of billed excess distance, which includes the residual matching difference.
Only the 5.15 km of the deviation is chargeable to the driver; the fare's waiting component is $0.00 and there is no surge (1.0×), so no other billed item is disturbed by the ruling.

The driver has 1,790 days of account history, a 4.84 rating and 344 trips in 90 days, and his only upheld dispute in 90 days is not a route dispute (route: 0), so this single deviation should not be treated as a repeated route-deviation pattern and no account flag is warranted on this record.
The rider's own 90-day record shows 2 disputes with 0 upheld, so the rider's overcharge complaint is not corroborated by any prior sustained finding.

weaknesses: The rider's consent (F8, 14:30) came after the off-route segment had already begun (F3, segment start 14:27), so under RD-5's 'before you go' test the passenger will argue the agreement does not cover this segment — the rider's complaint ('only mentioned the different route after he had already turned off') tracks exactly this fact pattern.

There is no traffic incident in the record to excuse the reroute (F12), and the only congestion evidence on the optimal route is a moderate speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the AYE (F10), which RD-4(b) says is at most corroborative and cannot exempt a segment on its own — so the driver cannot defend the 5.15 km deviation as a 'reasonable cause' reroute.

The magnitude of the deviation is large and hard to explain: +5.9 km / +69% (F1) over a 22.2-minute trip (F2), and the segment ran up to 1,194 m away from the optimal route (F3), facts the rider will use to argue the deviation was not a minor, unavoidable detour.

The driver's billing shows $8.35 of excess distance (F4) while the segment-level extra distance is 5.15 km (F3), so the rider will press for the larger figure; under RD-2 only meter units of the unexempted segment are refundable, which limits but does not eliminate the exposure (about $7.26).

We agree on the RD-2 quantum: 5.15 extra_km × $1.41/km (distance fare $20.43 ÷ 14.5 km) = $7.26, and we do not press for the $8.35 distance total, since RD-2 refunds meter units only (F3, F4, F6).

RD-6's threshold is met on the record the driver himself cites: his profile shows 1 upheld dispute in the last 90 days (F15), so once this deviation is upheld the condition 'route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1 plus this case' is satisfied and the account flag is an additional action, not a finding on its own.

The rider's substantive point is right on the timestamps: the agreement (F8, 14:30) post-dates the segment start (F3, 14:27), so RD-5's 'before you go' test is not met and I do not press full exemption for the segment.

Conceded: no incident was recorded near the route (F12) and the AYE record is only band 4 (30–39 km/h, F10), which RD-4(b) does not allow to exempt a segment on its own; my client's congestion explanation therefore does not defeat RD-2 liability.
